hook.line: Hernando never says "strong" when he can say something more vivid. Spanish speakers love a picture: it makes a description stick, and it is easier than finding the exact adjective.
hook.es: Mi abuelo es fuerte como un toro.
hook.en: My grandad is as strong as an ox.

rule:
Three easy frames for a picture instead of a plain adjective.

*Adjective + como + un/una + thing*: *fuerte como un toro*, *lento como una tortuga*. Same as English "as strong as an ox", without the first "as".

*Parece + un/una + thing*: *parece una caja*.

*Es como + verb*: *Es como tener un vigilante*.

Keep the *un* or *una*: *como tortuga* sounds wrong. Many comparisons are fixed, so don't swap the animal: strong is *toro*, slow is *tortuga*.
smallPrint: Teachers call these *símiles* (similes), and *parecer* here is a verb of appearance.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose the right word and type the whole sentence: Mi hermano es lento ___ una tortuga. (como / parece)
yourTurn.answer: Mi hermano es lento como una tortuga.
yourTurn.why: With an adjective in front, the link word is *como*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: My grandad is as strong as an ox.
yourTurn.answer: Mi abuelo es fuerte como un toro.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: That bag weighs as much as a brick.
yourTurn.answer: Esa bolsa pesa como un ladrillo.
yourTurn.why: With *pesar*, *como un ladrillo* works the same way.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: The apartment looks like a box.
yourTurn.why: *Parece* is followed directly by *un* or *una*, no *como*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: Tomás is as red as a tomato.
yourTurn.answer: Tomás está rojo como un tomate.
yourTurn.why: *Está* because it is how he looks right now.

yourTurn.prompt: Say it about your grandma: Mi abuelo es fuerte como un toro.
yourTurn.answer: Mi abuela es fuerte como un toro.
yourTurn.why: Only *abuela* changes; the fixed comparison stays *un toro*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: It's like having a security guard at home.
yourTurn.answer: Es como tener un vigilante en la casa.
yourTurn.why: *Es como* plus an infinitive describes an experience.

pitfalls.wrong: Mi hermano es lento como tortuga.
pitfalls.right: Mi hermano es lento como una tortuga.
pitfalls.why: Almost. Spanish keeps *un* or *una* in these comparisons.

pitfalls.wrong: Mi hermano es lento como un perro.
pitfalls.right: Mi hermano es lento como una tortuga.
pitfalls.why: These comparisons are fixed: for slow, Spanish always picks the turtle.

pitfalls.wrong: El apartamento parece como una caja.
pitfalls.why: Almost. English says "looks like", but *parece* already means that, so no *como*.

personal: Describe someone you know with a picture: *Mi amigo es… como un…* or *Mi casa parece un…*
